author: Tashner, [a son of John Charles Tashner Jr.]
title: What our father told us: J. C. Tashner Jr. at Pearl Harbor and after — family correspondence
notes:
One of Jay Tashner's sons, writing in August 2026, on his father's enlistment, family and war: the morning of 7 December in a barracks at Pearl Harbor, the rifle at the door, the days spent recovering bodies from the harbour, the carriers and destroyers, and the promotion he turned down. Supplied to this project by the writer's son. The account gives no author's name here because the material did not; he is identified only as one of Jay's sons.

Oral history at second hand, and the tier says so: this is what a man told his children, written down by one of them some sixty years after the last of it and eighty-five after the morning it opens with. It is cited for what Jay Tashner remembered and how his family holds it, never for a time, a place, a unit or a weapon. Its own hedges are kept where it makes them — "Jack died in 1967 I think", "about 1888", "about 1973" — because a hedge is evidence about evidence and promoting it to a fact by transcription is the failure this rung exists to name.

It disagrees with its author's brother in two places that the 1941 pack carries rather than resolves: on why Jay refused a commission, and on the shape of his service. It also carries an internal tension of its own — he enlists at seventeen on leaving high school, which puts it around 1938, and retires in 1958 after twenty-one years, which puts it around 1937. Neither is corrected here.
